To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
supplemental fibers are present in 3 of the 4 native menisci root attachments and contribute significantly to their ultimate failure strengths.

the posterior medial, posterior lateral, and anterior medial meniscal roots contain supplemental fibers that account for a significant percentage (up to 30%) of the root attachments and significantly contribute to the failure strengths and stiffness of the native roots.
supplemental fibers contribute to the biomechanics of the meniscal roots.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the biomechanical relevance of the meniscal roots and their contribution to knee joint stability.
the biomechanical behavior of the meniscal roots.
the structural properties of the native meniscal roots and how the presence of supplemental fibers contribute to the ultimate failure strengths of the root attachments.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the supplemental fibers are not biomechanically relevant and do not contribute significantly to the ultimate failure strength and attachment area of the root attachments.
the supplemental fibers of the PM, PL, AM meniscal roots contribute significantly to the failure strength and attachment area of the native meniscal roots.
the current surgical techniques for meniscus repair fail to reattach a significant portion of the meniscus attachment area.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the posterior medial, posterior lateral, and anterior medial meniscal roots contain a significant amount of supplemental fibers that significantly contribute to the biomechanically important properties of the root attachments.
the meniscal root attachments are complex and should be repaired with a technique that incorporates the most prominent, densely attached fibers, as well as supplemental peripheral attachments.

the posterior roots of the medial and lateral meniscus contain significant amounts of tissue that are not currently reattached during meniscal root repair surgery and that contribute to the overall strength of the native root attachments.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the most prominent, thickened portion of the meniscus is not the only attachment site of the meniscal roots.
the supplemental attachments of the PM, PL, AL, and AM roots are biomechanically significant.
the current surgical technique of reattaching the most prominent, central portion of the root fails to incorporate these supplemental fibers.
